mcqs.question: An interviewer asks 'design a chat app's mobile client.' What's the strongest first move, before proposing any architecture?
options: Immediately draw the full system architecture diagram, since that demonstrates technical depth fastest
Explicitly clarify scope out loud — 1:1 vs group chat, offline support, media attachments, encryption — since these substantially change the right design
Ask the interviewer to just specify every requirement upfront before saying anything
Assume the most common interpretation silently and proceed without discussing it
mcqs.explanation: Scope clarification is itself a signal of seniority and directly changes the right architecture — silently assuming one interpretation risks solving the wrong problem, and jumping straight to a diagram skips a step that shapes what that diagram should even contain. Asking the interviewer to enumerate everything upfront offloads the framing work that's actually the candidate's job to demonstrate.

mcqs.question: When a user taps send on a message, what should happen first in a well-designed chat client?
options: Wait for the server to acknowledge the message before showing it in the conversation view at all
Show a full-screen loading spinner until the network round trip finishes
Queue the message only after checking that the device currently has connectivity
Insert the message into the local database immediately in a pending state and render it right away, before the network send even completes
mcqs.explanation: This is optimistic UI applied to chat — inserting locally and rendering immediately is what makes sending feel instant regardless of connectivity, with the actual network send and acknowledgment happening afterward. Waiting for server acknowledgment or gating on connectivity before showing anything defeats the offline-first design this pattern is built on, and a full-screen spinner is exactly the laggy experience optimistic UI avoids.

mcqs.question: Why do chat apps typically use a push notification to trigger a fetch, rather than delivering the full message content directly inside the push payload, when the app is backgrounded?
options: Push notifications cannot be received while an app is backgrounded
This approach is purely a legacy convention with no current technical justification
A persistent connection is always maintained even while backgrounded, making push notifications unnecessary
Push payloads have real size limits and reliability caveats, so using them as a lightweight trigger for a regular API fetch is more robust than relying on the push to carry the actual content
mcqs.explanation: Push notification payloads have genuine size and reliability constraints, so using the push as a trigger to fetch the actual content via a normal API call is more robust than depending on the push itself to reliably deliver the full message. Push notifications are specifically designed to reach backgrounded apps, and persistent connections are generally not reliably maintained while backgrounded due to platform background execution limits.

mcqs.question: Why should a message's delivery state be modeled as an ordered state machine (pending -> sent -> delivered -> read) rather than several independent boolean flags?
options: Independent booleans use less memory and are always preferable for this reason alone
Boolean flags cannot represent more than two states, making them technically impossible to use here
An ordered state machine can enforce that the state never regresses backward due to an out-of-order network event, which independent booleans can't guarantee on their own
There is no practical difference between the two approaches
mcqs.explanation: A defined sequence of valid transitions lets the client reject an out-of-order update (a delivered event arriving after read) by construction, preventing a visible regression in the UI's checkmark — independent booleans have no inherent ordering guarantee against exactly this kind of race. Multiple booleans could technically represent the states, just without that ordering safety, and memory usage isn't the deciding factor here.

mcqs.question: An app shows a message's 'sent' checkmark the instant it's inserted into the local database, before any network request has been attempted. What's the risk?
options: This causes a compile-time type error since pending and sent must be handled identically
A user could believe a message was successfully sent when it hasn't actually left the device yet, especially under poor connectivity
There is no risk — pending and sent are functionally identical states for UI purposes
This only matters for group chats, never for 1:1 messaging
mcqs.explanation: Conflating pending and sent visually means a user has no way to distinguish 'queued locally' from 'confirmed by the server,' which matters most exactly when connectivity is poor and the gap between the two states is long enough to notice and be misled by. This is a real correctness/trust issue, not a compile-time concern, and it applies to 1:1 messaging just as much as group chat.

mcqs.question: A message send request times out client-side after the server actually processed it successfully. The client retries with no idempotency key. What's the visible result to the recipient?
options: The recipient sees the same message appear twice in the conversation
The recipient sees no message at all, since the timeout prevents delivery
The sender's app automatically detects and suppresses the duplicate before it's ever sent
The server automatically merges the two requests into one message regardless of idempotency key presence
mcqs.explanation: Without an idempotency key, the server has no way to recognize the retry as the same logical send, so it creates a second message record — visible to the recipient as a duplicate, a bug that's immediately obvious in a chat UI. There's no automatic client-side suppression or server-side merging without an explicit idempotency mechanism in place, and the message was actually delivered, not lost.
